en: The Śramaṇa Ji composed this treatise. [It states:
"Because other formations (saṃskāra) and other matter (rūpa) do not reach the nature of cognition (buddhi). The commentary states: "Cognition (buddhi) means discernment;

it is the general name for mind and mental factors (citta-caitta). Apart from the mental factors, there are the remaining formations, the external bases (bāhyāyatana), and non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa)."
Nor is it a real self,
because it lacks the nature of cognition,
just like space and so forth.
In this context, it is merely combined as a single measure;
however, there is no logical contradiction in treating the formations (*saṃskāra*) and form (*rūpa*), etc., as individual measures.
The method of *hetuvidyā* (logic) functions as a critique of others;
it states that [the self] is not of the nature of cognition (*buddhi*).

This does not mean that the nature of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) is being overturned or revealed as the nature of cognition; rather, [the opponent] asserts that [the self] is a real self (*ātman*).
This also serves to exclude [other] views;
it does not necessarily imply a fixed attachment.
Together with the seven types of inference, this refutes the first view.
Treatise:
From the perspective of the middle way, the self is devoid of the aggregates, up to being without action or reception.
Commentary: [As stated above.]
This refutes the calculations of the Sāṃkhya and others.
The *Pramāṇa* says:
"The self that is so calculated..."
There should be no performing or experiencing [of karma],
because they are not subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*),
just like space and so forth.
In this passage, only the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the similar example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) are present;
the reason (*hetu*) is as previously indicated,
and therefore it is omitted here.
The text uses a single measure to refute the calculation of a "middle.
Now, to assist in this refutation, it says:
"The self that is calculated..."
It must not be a real self,
because it is not subsumed within the aggregates (skandhas),
just like space and so forth.
From this point downward, each case should be considered accordingly.
[The] treatise states:
"Finally, because it is neither [of those two], it is not a real self."
The commentary states:
This refutes the Vātsīputrīyas and others.
According to their tenet, the self (ātman) is neither identical to nor separate from the aggregates (skandhas) upon which it depends.
Nevertheless, it possesses a distinct substantial entity that is neither permanent nor impermanent,
as described in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, fascicle 29, in the discussion on the meaning of the "difficult-to-rely-upon" (*aniśrita*).
Now, this is explained:
"basis" (āśraya) means that which is relied upon;
it is designated upon the aggregates (skandha).

Because it is neither identical nor distinct, I fear that a detailed exposition would be too prolix; thus, I shall not describe it further. As for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is said:
The "self" that you grasp must not be a real self.
The reason is as follows:
It is permitted that [the self] is established in dependence upon the aggregates, because it is neither identical to nor separate from the aggregates,
just like a jar or a bowl. Therefore,
the term "dharma" used here should not refer to a real self.
To distinguish true suchness:
although true suchness depends upon the aggregates, it is neither identical to nor separate from them;
yet, because it is not a real self, there is no lack of definiteness.
In the context of the reason (*hetu*), it is asserted that there is no fault of being either one [of the two] or both.
The sequence of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth is explained according to the meaning of the text.
They [the opponents] maintain that jars and the like are established in dependence upon the four sense-objects (*viṣaya*) and the aggregates (*skandha*).
However, because it is neither identical to nor separate from the four sensory objects,
it is used as a metaphor.
Treatise.
Furthermore, since it cannot be said whether [the self] reaches [this state] or is not the self,
the commentary states:
"They establish five dharma-treasuries."
Regarding the three periods of time, the unconditioned,
and that which is inexpressible, they conceive of this self as being eternally impermanent and inexpressible as either conditioned or unconditioned.
Now, the Master of the Treatise directly uses "self" and "non-self" as the illustrative example.
One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
"The self that you postulate..."
It should not be said that this is the self,
because it is admitted that what is inexpressible cannot be either conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*),
like the hair of a tortoise; thus, by means of two formal inferences (*pramāṇa*), the third position is refuted.
If one refutes the "neither-nor" position,
the opponent's own school also asserts that the self is not the "neither-nor" position,
as it cannot be said to be either self or non-self; thus, you commit the fallacy of contradicting your own position (*pratijñā-saṃnyāsa*).
Furthermore, there is no similar example [to support it].
Now, in refuting the "self," we simultaneously explain the "non-self.
It must be definitively stated that this [self] is the aggregates (skandhas).
It should not be said that it is not an aggregate (skandha).
Furthermore, the proof states:
"The self (ātman) which you maintain..."
The meaning of the aggregates as "self" or "non-self" should likewise be inexpressible,
since you admit they are inexpressible—
just like the meanings of "conditioned" and "unconditioned. Now, the intent of this passage is not to allow them to enter into either the category of "self" or "non-self."
Therefore, there is no fault. According to the treatise,
the real self as they have conceived it is not established.
The commentary states:
This is the summary.
By combining ten types of inference (*anumāna*), these three views are refuted.
Treatise:
Furthermore, all that is grasped as "reaching" (prāpti) is devoid of thought.
Commentary states:
From here below begins the third section, which generally refutes the two aforementioned specific attachments to a self.
This contains four parts;
first, [the refutation of] that which possesses volition.
The refutation by way of the absence of thought;
second, the refutation by way of the presence of activity versus the absence of activity.
3. The object of the view of self;
the refutation of the object of the view of self.
4. The object of the views of both self and non-self.
The view of self is not destroyed by its own conditions.
Here, "all" is said because one is inquiring collectively about all the selves previously asserted. "That which possesses deliberation" is a question directed at the Sāṃkhya.
They assert that the essence of the *puruṣa* (self) is consciousness; therefore, there is no one who lacks deliberation.
[The author] questions the Vaiśeṣikas and others, yet the Sāṃkhyas maintain this view.
The essential nature of the Puruṣa is eternally abiding.
With the exception of Prakṛti, although the essential natures of the twenty-three principles are eternal,
they still possess the characteristic of transformation and impermanence.
Now, if you challenge us, we should likewise maintain that those twenty-three principles (tattvas) must all possess a nature that undergoes transformation and is impermanent.
Treatise.
"If there is volition up to and including volition.
The commentary states:
"Your self-essence."
It must be a transformational impermanence,
because its activity may sometimes fail to arise,
just as is accepted in the case of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth.
If one does not rely on its function, it would be difficult to cause its essence to undergo transformation as well;
thus, there would be no similar instance (*sapakṣa*),
because they do not admit that cessation constitutes impermanence.
If it were used directly,
there would be the fallacy of contradiction (pratijñā-virodha), because its function as an object of thought does not arise at all times,
even though its essential nature is eternal.
Because this [reason] is impermanent,
there is no fault of being inconclusive,
for it is not commonly accepted [as such].
Furthermore, according to this principle, function should also be impermanent;
thus, it is also possible for the characteristic to be identical [to the entity]. Thus says the Treatise:
"If there is no volition, even upon arrival [at fruition], one does not receive the fruit.
The commentary states:
"This refutes the Vaiśeṣika and other schools."
The meaning is easy to understand.
The *Pramāṇa* says:
"Do you truly [perceive] a self?"
It would be incapable of performing actions and incapable of experiencing their results,
because you admit it lacks volition,
just like space.
The two types of inference regarding the performance of action and the experiencing of its fruit are as follows.
That is to say, with the exception of the Sāṃkhya school, all other theories postulating a *puruṣa* (self) are refuted in the same manner. Thus concludes the treatise.
Therefore, both the [subject] "self" and its underlying principle are unestablished.
The commentary states:
This is the double conclusion regarding the two [points].
Treatise:
Furthermore, all that is grasped as "reaching" (prāpti) is devoid of causal efficacy.
Commentary: [As follows:]
Furthermore, this second pair again refutes the previous explanation;
this constitutes the definitive inquiry.
Treatise:
"If there were an active function [of arising], it would necessarily be impermanent.
The commentary states:
"The various masters formulate their calculations and assertions differently."
In terms of function,
the function of experiencing is likewise reckoned to exist.
As the *Upayoga* states:
The self must be impermanent because it possesses activity,
just like the hands, feet, and so forth.
If one considers the Sāṃkhya school,
transformation is like that of the hands and so forth;
if one considers the Vaiśeṣika and other schools...
The phrase "perishing like the feet and so forth" is consistent in its syntactic structure, yet its underlying meaning differs.
Space and suchness are devoid of any functional activity.
Therefore, there is no uncertainty.
[The] treatise says:
If there is no activity, both [theories] will fail to be established.
The commentary states:
There is no such thing as a self that acts or experiences.
Even for the Sāṃkhya teacher, if there were no agent of action, it would likewise be called "useless."
If there were movement, transformation, activity, or functional efficacy,
these would be non-existent both in terms of their superior nature and their numerical occurrence,
because they are explained by means of ten propositions.
Because the son of the Vaiśya [Vatsagotra] and others possess movement and change,
they belong to the former category;
the rest belong to the latter category.
Furthermore, regarding the time when liberation is attained,
as for the "self" that is postulated by various [schools], it is entirely useless. The formal proof (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:
The self that is grasped [as real] must not be a real self,
because it lacks causal activity.
Just as with rabbit horns and the like,
space is also [non-existent],
because it lacks functional activity.
The scriptural statement that there is no real self does not mean that [the self] does not exist as a reality; therefore,
that True Suchness (tathatā) does not incur the fault of being indeterminate.
If that is so, why speak of permanence, bliss, self, and purity?
This is not a fixed, real self,
for its nature is beyond verbal expression.
The statement "I" is a mere conventional designation.
This [notion] is useless, and all such attachments are indeed false.
There is not a single teacher who maintains that the self is useless.
However, since the refutation concerns the function of "action" (kriyā) and "efficacy" (śakti), it can be considered a valid objection.
Alternatively, there is a refutation that interchanges "action" and "reception" (vedanā);
that is to say, one should respond as follows.
The *sāṃkhya* and other [schools] maintain that the self (*ātman*) should not be a real self,
because it lacks the function of being solely an agent.
The Ātman as [conceived by] the Vaiśeṣikas and others should not be a real self,
because it lacks the function of being merely an experiencer.
Regarding things such as the horns of a rabbit, what is negated here is merely the function of being an experiencer (*vedaka*).
It is not that the nature of being an experiencer alone is accepted as a real self (*ātman*);
for if it were so, then the foundational consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the *sāṃkhya* self would also have to be real selves.
It is merely stated that the rabbit's horn lacks the function of being experienced;
it is not said that the rabbit's horn exists as an agent of action or experience.
Therefore, this is not a fault.
Because the proponents of Pramāṇa employ the method of negation (paryudāsa),
the conclusion of the text is easy to understand;
therefore, it is not explained separately.
Treatise:
Furthermore, do all those things which are grasped reach the objects to which they are directed? Commentary:
It is said in response:
This is the third [section], which also collectively challenges the preceding views of both internal and external paths.
The treatise states:
"If it were not the view of a self... up to... knowing that a real self exists."
The commentary states:
This refutes the fundamental tenet that the self is the object of the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). The formal argument (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:
That self which you postulate...
It should not be the self,
because it is admitted to be the object of the view of non-self (*anātma-dṛṣṭi*),
just like form, sound, and so forth. Furthermore, the meaning of this proof is as follows:
If you could take my mind and its mental factors as objects,
you would not know me, because [knowing them] is not the view of a self.
As in the case of taking other minds as objects, although there is no textual justification,
it is established by reasoning,
such as in the case of a mind and its mental factors taking *tathatā* (suchness) as their object.
Although one does not necessarily form a conceptual understanding of suchness,
one succeeds in taking suchness as an object;
the mind that takes the self as its object is likewise the same as that.
Although one does not form the conceptual understanding of a self,
what prevents one from taking the self as an object?
Although the mind that takes suchness as its object does not form the conceptual understanding of suchness.
True Suchness is still called the object-condition of the mind;
although the view of self does not produce the cognition of a self,
that self should be called the object-condition of the view of self.
Therefore, this explanation is provided to assist in refuting that error.
Treatise:
If it were the view of a self, [it would persist] until one attains knowledge of reality as it is.
The commentary states:
This refutes the "self" as the objective referent (*ālambana*) of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
The formal inference (*pramāṇa*) is as follows:
The view of self with respect to what is conditioned by the self should not be a perverted view,
because it knows [the object] as it truly is.
Because it conforms to its object—
just as the mind that takes form and so forth as its object— the teachings held by non-Buddhists and followers of the Lesser Vehicle who cling to a self all admit that the view of self,
though conforming to its object, is in essence a perversion.
By severing [these], one becomes a sage.
Although the mind of non-self does not correspond to the object,
it is called "non-inverted" because it opposes defilement.
If one takes the true mind as an object and conceives of it as having existence, this is attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
If one conceives of it as non-existent,
although this does not accord with reality, one nevertheless attains sainthood by means of that cause.
Treatise:
If this is so, how does it proceed to the praise of non-self? Commentary:
[It proceeds as follows.]
"Ultimate teaching" refers to the teaching of ultimate reality,
as in the *Viṃśatikā*.
If you say that this view of self is likewise not an inversion,
for what reason does your own teaching state that because the view of self is defiled, it must be abandoned to become a noble one?
Since it is through the view of non-self that one can attain nirvāṇa,
the view of self is disparaged and the view of non-self is praised.
This constitutes a refutation based on the internal contradictions found within other schools.
The Treatise states: "The view of non-self leads to sinking into the cycle of birth and death.
The Commentary says:
In your own school,
you yourselves say that those who give rise to the view of a self sink into the cycle of birth and death because of this defilement.
The arising of the view of non-self can realize nirvāṇa;
because it is pure,
this objection is established from the perspective of that very school.
Treatise:
How could it be that those with false views fall into the cycle of birth and death?
Commentary states:
This summarizes the objection:
the view of selflessness is a false means for realizing nirvāṇa,
because it does not accord with its objective referent.
I see that this [view] is precisely what causes one to sink into the cycle of birth and death,
for it conforms to objective conditions.
This same objection is also raised in the *Śata-śāstra*.
Treatise:
Furthermore, regarding all views of self up to those that take other minds as their object.
Commentary:
The following fourth section provides a general refutation of the preceding teachers.
It is unnecessary to speak separately of the wisdom of defilement and purity;
rather, it concerns the view of a self that you have described.
Now, all of these are refuted;
there is no fault of mutual correspondence.
One should formulate the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
Your view takes me as its object;
it does not take a real self as its object.
This is the thesis.
Because it has an object of perception,
it is a cause; for example,
the mind that takes external forms such as the self as its object.
This is an analogy.
One should understand that the sequence of the text is as follows:
however, according to those [schools], all [views] involve the view of self (ātmadṛṣṭi), yet they do not arise by taking a self as their object.
As the Sāṃkhyas say, the view of a creator self (vedavādin) does not arise based on a real self,
because it is a mere false imputation.
The same should be understood by analogy for the other views when compared with one another.
Therefore, in this school, there must be a distinction:
your respective individual statements that the view taking a self as its object is not a false conceptualization (parikalpa) do not establish it as a real entity (dharmin).
The intention of the Mahāyāna here is to demonstrate that all views which take a self as their object arise solely by not apprehending a real self.
There is no need for further analysis.
This refutes the idea that the cognitive faculty arises by not taking a self as its object;
next, it refutes the notion that the object of cognition must necessarily be a real self.
Treatise:
The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is like that of other dharmas.
Commentary: [As follows].
The proof for this is as follows:
"That which is the object of my perception is certainly not a real self" is the thesis.
Because it is an object of cognition (*ālambana*),
it is a cause,
just like other phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
This is an analogy.
Within the [proponent's] thesis, one should likewise differentiate as before,
because each of those [schools] respectively conceives of an object of the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) that is not a real self.
Treatise:
Therefore, from the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) up to various conceptual constructions (*vicitra-parikalpa*).
Commentary states:
This is the conclusion of the verse.
It is as in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.
The sixteen great treatises all maintain that the images which are the manifestations of one's own mind serve as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*);
for there is not a single "self" that constitutes these manifested aspects.
These are merely the aggregates transformed by consciousness as its object;
because each aggregate is distinct,
they are called "the various aggregates."
That is to say, because one calculates and conceptualizes these various aggregates in manifold ways,
this differs from what is taught in the Hīnayāna.
Treatise.
However, there are briefly two types of self-grasping.
[The commentary] states:
"In the refutation of the self..."
From here below is the fourth [section],
which explains those grasped [objects] as being both conceptual and innate.
If one were to divide this into three categories, this would be the second.
Within this, there are two parts.
First, the individual explanation of the two types of grasping;
second, "Thus, all such grasping at a self as has been described... and so forth.
This provides a general explanation of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*).
The first part consists of three sections.
The first [section] indicates the grasping and enumerates its categories.
Second, the enumeration of names;
third, the detailed explanation.
This is the first [section]. There are two types of general enumerations.
The various categories herein are as explained in the separate chapter:
namely, the confusion regarding the general and specific aspects of the truths,
and the existence or non-existence of the various consciousnesses.
Regarding the stages of subduing and severing,
they are comprised within nine grades;
these consist of those that are subdued and those that are not subdued.
Regarding the coarse and subtle stages of the abandonment of the two types of grasping—
those concerning persons and phenomena— the twenty categories of conceptual and innate [grasping], and so forth,
should each be understood individually as explained below.
Although no single sentient being possesses twenty such phrases and so forth,
it is nonetheless possible for them to exist within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
As for what is called "clinging to a self" (ātma-grāha):
This demonstrates that it is not merely vision;
for the treatise states that all mind and mental factors are termed "grasping.
This [grasping] is twofold: first, the innate (*sahaja*); second, the conceptual (*vikalpita*).
The commentary states:
This enumeration refers to those distinctions that arise simultaneously with the body; they are called "co-emergent" (*sahaja*).
The subsequent imputation that gives rise to [the notion of] birth is called "arising from discrimination.
This is explained separately below.
Treatise:
It is called "innate" (*sahaja*) because it has existed since birth.
[The commentary] states:
From here below, there is a detailed explanation.
First, the innate [afflictions] are explained;
later, the conceptualized [afflictions] are explained. Regarding the former, there are three parts.
First, the meaning of the innate is explained.
Second, it reveals their distinctions;
third, it clarifies the stage of abandonment.
[These arise] solely by depending on internal seeds.
To say that it is "always co-existent with the body" while being distinct from the objects of discrimination:
this explains the meaning of its co-existence. To say that it "transforms":
this explains the meaning of its arising.
The remainder of the text is easy to understand.
The treatise states:
"This, moreover, is of two kinds... up to: grasping it as a real self."
The commentary states:
The preceding section provides a general explanation of co-nascence;
the following section provides a detailed analysis of its distinctions. Regarding "constant continuity":
"Manifesting the meaning of constant arising" refers to [the manas] being in the seventh [consciousness].
"Manifesting the basis of grasping" refers to taking the eighth [consciousness] as its object.
"Manifesting the appearance of its own mind" refers to the objective sphere.
This reveals that the eighth [consciousness] does not directly adhere [to objects].
As for those who grasp it as a real self, because their cognition does not correspond to the object, grasping arises.
They have not yet attained the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Within the seventh consciousness, the grasping at a self arises constantly;
it is called "perpetually continuous" because its objects of perception are always present.
It is not like the grasping within the sixth mental consciousness.
For what reason does this continuity reside only in the seventh?
Briefly stated, there are two reasons.
First, because their objects are limited:
namely, the eye, ear, nose, and so forth;
and the mental consciousness, the eight [consciousnesses], and the seven [mental] consciousnesses.
Alternatively, there may be nine, eight, seven, five, four, or three conditions due to the reduction of certain factors.
If the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
the co-existent condition (*sahabhū-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) are added, these are further increased accordingly.
Because it relies on few conditions,
the seventh [consciousness] maintains a continuous self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*) unlike the others,
as explained in the seventh fascicle regarding the number of conditions.
The second [type of knowledge] is profound both by way of its mode of activity (*ākāra*) and its continuity;
the eighth is continuous but not profound.
The sixth consciousness is deep but not continuous;
the five sensory consciousnesses are neither deep nor continuous;
the seventh consciousness possesses both.
Therefore, it is only the seventh consciousness and no others.
The fundamental nature of this seventh consciousness takes the eighth consciousness as its object.
Because it resembles that which is unitary and permanent,
and resembles the characteristics of a real self,
the seventh [consciousness] constantly functions by taking the eighth [consciousness] as its object.
Within the appearance of the image, there is likewise no real self;
it merely resembles the eighth consciousness and is the appearance of one's own mind as the seventh consciousness.
If explained from the perspective of the views, it is called defiled indeterminate;
if explained from the perspective of its fundamental nature, it is called pure indeterminate.
Because both defilement and purity are admitted, it is produced from a variety of causes.
To grasp the appearance manifested by one's own mind as being permanent and unitary is called "grasping" because it does not correspond to the object.
That which does not correspond to the fundamental substance is called "grasping."
The five consciousnesses should also be termed "with-grasping" (sopādāna),
insofar as they take the dependent nature as their characteristic by way of images.
If considered in terms of what is grasped,
that which manifests according to one's own mind is also called a "sign" (nimitta).
This refers to those who take the eighth consciousness as their object.
This is the essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Below, one should understand from this that the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) also has two [aspects].
Treatise:
"Second, there is the intermittent [grasping] up to the grasping of it as a real self.
Commentary:
This exists within the sixth consciousness.
This clarifies where they are held.
The sixth mode of activity is profound yet intermittent;
the seventh is both profound and uninterrupted.
The five consciousnesses are severed but not deeply;
the eighth consciousness is neither deep nor severed.
Therefore, this self-grasping exists only within the six consciousnesses.
Regarding the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*):

this demonstrates that they are the objective domain of the co-emergent view of self (*sahaja-ātma-dṛṣṭi*), and thus do not take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object. In the Sarvāstivāda school, all afflictions (*kleśa*) are termed "clinging" (*upādāna*).
The aggregates arise from grasping, or they are capable of producing grasping;
therefore, they are called "aggregates of grasping" (*upādānaskandha*). Now, in the Mahāyāna, as explained in the Abhidharma:
Clinging (*upādāna*) is defined as sensual craving (*kāmarāga*);
it has craving alone as its essence,
consisting of a defiled longing for the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
The aggregates (skandhas) can produce grasping (upādāna);
the aggregates arise from grasping;
the establishment of the aggregates is termed grasping.
The characteristics of the activity [of the view of self] are revealed through the general and specific conditions of the aggregates (*skandha*).
Taking the five aggregates as a whole to be the self is called "general";
taking the five aggregates individually to be the self is called "specific."
It is not the twenty-fold view of self (ātma-dṛṣṭi) and so forth;
for the twenty-fold view is merely conceptual construction (vikalpa).
Within the seventh consciousness, it only takes the distinct aggregate of consciousness as its object.
The mode of activity (ākāra) is constantly fixed on the view of self as a single category;
one cannot discuss its being general or particular.
Therefore, it differs from this [view].
The seventh consciousness relies solely upon the eighth as its objective aspect (*nimitta*).
While it is said that its own mental images arise based on the essential nature (*svabhāva*) [of the eighth],
the "aspects of the five aggregates of clinging" mentioned herein may be taken either collectively or individually.
This is the sixth essential nature.
That which arises as a characteristic of one's own mind is the characteristic of the image.
This reveals that although conditions are not attached [to a self], one falsely gives rise to the notion of a self.
Furthermore, because the essence of the sixth [consciousness] is not fixed as a single phenomenon, it is not mentioned separately.
In fact, they also possess a non-non-essential nature because they are co-emergent. Therefore,
what has been stated— that the five aggregates of clinging and so forth all give rise to images— is established.
Treatise:
These two forms of self-grasping can only be eliminated upon reaching that stage.
Commentary:
This is the third passage.
It clarifies the locus where subtle attachments are severed;
beginningless habitual practice makes their essence and characteristics subtle and hidden.
Therefore, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states:
"Because it follows along with present activity from afar,

Treatise: Therefore, the sūtra proceeds to state that the five aggregates of clinging arise. Commentary: The sūtra states: "Monks, what are the five aggregates of clinging? They are as follows: the form aggregate of clinging, the feeling aggregate of clinging, the perception aggregate of clinging, the formations aggregate of clinging, and the consciousness aggregate of clinging. What is the form aggregate of clinging? It refers to whatever is form, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; distant or near. Specifically, it includes the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements. What are the four great elements? They are the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element. What is the earth element? It is the quality of solidity within the internal body, whether it be long, short, square, round, coarse, fine, red, white, black, blue, yellow, or reddish-yellow. It is that which is grasped by the self, or that which is not grasped by the self. What is the water element? It is the quality of liquidity within the internal body, whether it be tears, pus, blood, sweat, mucus, saliva, nasal mucus, fat, grease, marrow, urine, or other such substances. It is that which is grasped by the self, or that which is not grasped by the self. What is the fire element? It is the quality of heat within the internal body, whether it be that which warms, that which burns, that which consumes food and drink, or that which digests what has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted. It is that which is grasped by the self, or that which is not grasped by the self. What is the wind element? It is the quality of motion within the internal body, whether it be upward-moving winds, downward-moving winds, winds in the flanks, winds in the belly, winds in the limbs, in-breath, out-breath, or other such winds. It is that which is grasped by the self, or that which is not grasped by the self. This is called the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element. Furthermore, whatever form exists internally or externally, whether past, future, or present; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; distant or near—all such form is collectively termed the form aggregate of clinging. What is the feeling aggregate of clinging? It refers to whatever feeling there is, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; distant or near. Specifically, it includes feeling born of contact with the eye, feeling born of contact with the ear, feeling born of contact with the nose, feeling born of contact with the tongue, feeling born of contact with the body, and feeling born of contact with the mind. Whether it be feeling born of pleasant contact, feeling born of painful contact, or feeling born of neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact—whether it be past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; distant or near—all such feeling is collectively termed the feeling aggregate of clinging. What is the perception aggregate of clinging? It refers to whatever perception there is, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; distant or near. Specifically, it includes the perception of forms, the perception of sounds, the perception of odors, the perception of tastes, the perception of tangibles, and the perception of mental phenomena. What is the formations aggregate of clinging? It refers to whatever formations there are, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; distant or near. Specifically, it includes contact, volition, initial application, sustained application, faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, regret, sleep, initial application, sustained application, non-regret, non-sleep, non-initial-application, non-sustained-application, vitarka, vicāra, and other such formations associated with the mind. Whether they be past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; distant or near—all such formations are collectively termed the formations aggregate of clinging. What is the consciousness aggregate of clinging? It refers to whatever consciousness there is, whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; distant or near. Specifically, it includes eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. Whether it be consciousness of the past, consciousness of the future, or consciousness of the present; consciousness of the internal, consciousness of the external, or consciousness of both internal and external; consciousness of the gross, consciousness of the subtle, or consciousness of both gross and subtle; consciousness of the inferior, consciousness of the superior, or consciousness of both inferior and superior; consciousness of the distant, consciousness of the near, or consciousness of both distant and near—all such consciousness is collectively termed the consciousness aggregate of clinging. This [conjunction] is of three types:

One strikes the drum with the hand.
The conjunction produced by the movement of the hand is karma;
karma is movement.
Second, they are produced by karma,
because both hands join together and move. Third,
they are produced by the conjunction of three factors.

Just as the arising of a sprout and the like involves no motion, so too is this the conjunction produced when [an object] truly meets with space and so forth. That which exists prior to the arrival of two things at a location is called separation (*viyoga*).
This also has three types.
The first two are reversals of conjunction, as can be understood from the previous discussion.
The third is arising through separation.
First, a real fruit is produced; then, due to the arrival of other conditions, the fruit undergoes disjunction and perishes, becoming empty and separated.
This produced disjunction is called "disjunction-born" (*visamyogaja*). It depends upon real entities such as numbers (one, two, etc.), time, and direction.
That which is depended upon by remote cognition is termed "that-nature" (tadātmatā).
Because this object is one and that object is two, it belongs to number.
Because it is "at this time" and "at that time," it belongs to time.

Because it pertains to this direction and that direction, it belongs to the category of spatial orientation (*dis*). One should understand its characteristics by reversing the nature of that [direction]. There are two kinds of cognition:
first, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
second, inference (*anumāna*).
That is to say, when the real [objects] such as form and so forth come into contact with the sense organs and so forth,
the arising of a cognition is termed "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*).
The intended meaning of this school is that the visual organ emits light rays and only then apprehends the object of form.
Just as a lamp illuminates objects,
the four objects— sound, fragrance, taste, and touch— are only apprehended once they reach their respective sense faculties.
Therefore, one sees a bell being struck from afar, yet the sound is heard only after a long interval.
Sound must enter the ear before it can be heard;
when the faculty and the proximate object come into contact,
there arises the production of cognition.
This "apprehension of characteristics" (lakṣaṇa-pariccheda) is the essence of direct perception (pratyakṣa).
There are two kinds of inference (anumāna):
first, inference based on seeing similarity (sādharmya-anumāna).
One perceives that which is not contradictory [to the probandum] and infers it from the thesis and the result,
such as when perceiving smoke, one infers the presence of fire.
Second, inference based on non-perception of identity:
one infers the thesis and its result by perceiving a contrary phenomenon.
For example, when hail is seen, one infers the destruction of the crops.

Seeing the damage to the crops due to wind and hail is called "suffering. That which is agreeable is called "pleasure. The longing for forms and so forth is called "desire. The harming of forms and so forth is called "hatred. When one is about to perform an action, there first arises "exertion" (*vīrya*).
This is called diligence (*vīrya*); it is the nature of exertion.

The cause of falling is called heaviness (*gurutva*). The cause of the flowing of earth, water, and fire is called fluidity (*dravatva*). The cause of cohesion for earth and the other elements is called moisture (*sneha*). There are two kinds of motion (*gati*).
First is the cause of recollection (*smṛti-hetu*); second is the cause of formation (*abhinirvṛtti-hetu*).
The specific distinctions arising from the repeated practice of the operation of present and inferential cognition are called the cause of recollection.
It is the seed of wisdom.
The functional efficacy produced by karma such as casting or throwing is called the "efficient cause" (kāraṇa-hetu).
Volitional formations (saṃskāra) are this functional efficacy.

first, those that can transform (*pravartaka*).
That is to say, one obtains the cause for a desirable body,

That is to say, it is the cause of joy based on the correct knowledge that takes detachment as its object;
it is the supramundane cause,
the primary cause of correct knowledge, which enables one to obtain a body within saṃsāra that is not to be craved.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that this refers to the category-meaning of "universal sameness" (*sāmānyapadārtha*). As for the essence of the category of "particularity" (*viśeṣa*), it always subsists in substances (*dravya*).

this restates the opponent's position.

Now, to refute this:
who allows that the substance of sand or copper receives water or medicine?
This implies that the substance of sand itself does not receive water.
It enters only into the empty space between two atoms,
not into the substance of a single atom. Likewise,
the matter of the fruit should also enter the empty space between two ultimate atoms.
It does not enter into the substance of a single atom;
the same applies to medicine entering copper.
This refers precisely to the creation of gold, brass, and stone.
This means that when a medicinal substance is placed within copper and it is transformed into gold,
the medicine merely enters the interstitial spaces of the copper.
"It does not enter into the atoms;
this is the tenet of our school.
This clarifies the meaning of "not entering. Below, the objection is raised from the perspective of that very tenet.
If the resultant form were present within the atoms that serve as its cause,
it would be separated from them— just as sand receives water—
meaning that the water would enter into the sand.
The two types of sand are separated by a great distance;
it is not that a minute amount of water has entered into the midst of the sand.
Thus says one measure.
In your school, water enters the sand;
it must be distinct from that which is not one,
because you admit that water enters into it.

Just as two grains of sand [do not enter one another], or as two atoms [do not enter] the interior of the parents' atoms, so too [the atoms] should be distinct and not one, because you admit that they enter within.
Or, like water entering sand, [they would be absorbed]. Thirdly, two atoms would have to touch one another.
Just as when coarse objects strike one another, their substances do not interpenetrate and they immediately disperse;
why then do you say that the resultant form enters into the causal atoms?
If it were so, the substance of the causal atoms would necessarily disperse.
Because it is touched by subtle [objects] that serve as its effects,
just as coarse objects strike one another;
furthermore, it is like medicinal herbs cast into molten copper.
They enter into the interstices between them.
Two atoms do not enter one another;
although they occupy these interstices, [they remain distinct].
Regarding the medicinal substance that causes copper atoms to transform into gold,
the *Pramāṇa* states:
"Even if one were to grant that the color of the effect enters into the intervals between the causal atoms..."

Furthermore, that cause [the atom] must likewise undergo transformation and differ from its original state, because it is admitted to enter into the interior of the atom, just as medicine transforms copper.
Therefore, the treatise states: "It should be distinct from that which undergoes transformation. This is precisely what is meant.
Water enters sand and separates from it;
or they separate by striking one another;
medicinal substances enter copper and transform it.
Because it has departed from its original state, it is not one;
because it undergoes transformation, it is not eternal.
Your atom should likewise be so.
It is neither unitary nor eternal,
like copper, sand, and so forth.
